title: Śrīdhara Svāmī literal English — Canto 4, chapter 3, complete checkpoint
grouping_note: Śrīdhara gives a single syntactic explanation of verses 4.3.5–7. Its complete three-verse range is retained; other entries correspond to individually numbered source glosses.

entries.text: In the third chapter, Satī, wishing to see the festivities of her father's sacrifice and intending to go, is restrained by Maheśa with reasons drawn from proper conduct. ‘While they were living’ means while they continued to remain alive; it is from the root dhṛṅ, ‘to remain.’

Although a sacrifice without Rudra is not possible, Dakṣa excluded Rudra through enmity and pride. The reason for his enmity has been stated; now he states the cause of his pride. When he was consecrated to authority over the progenitors, pride, that is, arrogance, arose in him.

Out of pride he ‘overpowered those established in Brahman,’ that is, he disregarded those accompanied by their Lord. The injunction says, ‘Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava’; thus he began the latter after performing the Vājapeya.

‘Having performed the auspicious preliminaries’ means ‘having performed the auspicious rites.’ By saying ‘together with their husbands,’ it is stated that the wives were honored again, even though their husbands had already been honored beforehand with gifts and the like.

The three verses are connected thus: hearing the aerial travelers speaking of the great festivities of her father's sacrifice, and seeing near her own residence the excellent women of the lesser gods, Gandharvas and the like, going there, Satī eagerly spoke to her husband, the Lord of beings. What kind of women? They used aerial cars as vehicles and were accompanied by their beloved husbands; they had niṣkas, ornamental medallions, at their necks and wore beautiful garments. Their eyes were restless and their earrings were polished and shining.
‘Set in motion’ means ‘begun.’ O Vāma, O Śiva, if you desire it, then let us also go there. The sacrifice has not yet finished, since these gods are still going there.

She reveals her eagerness with the six verses beginning ‘At that sacrifice.’ I wish to accept, together with you, the paribarha, ornaments and other articles given by my parents. In the alternative reading ‘honored,’ I desire the gifts bestowed by them.

‘Sisters’ means female siblings; ‘equal to their husbands’ means similar to their husbands. ‘Of softened mind’ means one whose heart is moist with affection. ‘I whose mind has long been eager’ means I, whose mind has been longing for a long time, shall see them. O Mṛḍa! ‘The banner raised by the great sages’ means the sacrifice, visible and foremost among sacrifices like a banner set up in their midst. Alternatively, it means the banner or sacrificial post erected at the sacrifice.

If one asks what wonder there is in that place that makes you so eager, she says ‘In you.’ O Unborn One! This universe, a wondrous thing, shines forth in you alone, fashioned by your māyā. Hence, although you do not regard it as wondrous, I am a woman whose nature is to be eager, and I do not know your true nature; therefore I am helpless and distressed. O Bhava, I desire to see my birth-land, the place where I was born.

She expresses her wish to see by the argument ‘How much more?’ in the two verses beginning ‘Look.’ O Abhava! You have not tasted the pain of separation from friends: that is the sense. Look, even women who are unrelated to us are going, accompanied by their husbands, in groups. Their aerial cars adorn the sky. O blue-throated one! This suggests that you even swallowed poison to show favor to others.

O foremost of the gods, when she hears of festivities at her father's home, how could a daughter's body not stir to see them? But how can we go without being invited? In reply she says that people go, even uninvited, to a friend's house, and to the houses of a husband, a teacher and a father. ‘House’ means dwelling; the short vowel is a usage of the sages.

O immortal one, therefore be gracious. You are able to fulfill this wish of mine. She further expresses his compassion: even though you have great knowledge, you have placed and borne me in half of your own body, whence you are known as Ardhanārīśvara. Therefore show me favor, as I have requested you.
‘Addressed’ means entreated. ‘Who’ refers to Dakṣa, who uttered those ill-spoken arrows that pierce vital spots; Satī caused Śiva to remember them.

What you said, ‘They go even uninvited,’ is indeed proper. But that is so only if those relatives have not conceived a fault through pride in the body and the anger arising from it. ‘Those whose sight has not produced a fault’ means those whose vision is not directed toward an imagined or superimposed fault.

One might ask how Dakṣa, possessing learning and other virtues, could find fault with great persons like you. He answers: when discrimination is destroyed precisely by learning and the other qualities, such people do not see the brilliance of the greatest persons. How can qualities destroy discrimination? For good people they are virtues and causes of discernment; for those who are not good, they become the opposite, defects. Accordingly, the pride ‘I am learned, an ascetic,’ and so forth is borne or nourished by those qualities, and their vision is corrupted by that pride.

‘Out of regard for one's own people’ means through seeing them as relatives. One should not go to, or visit, their homes. He explains their unstable minds: they look with a crooked intention and with eyebrows raised or arched and eyes filled with anger. ‘With raised eyebrows’ can be construed either as a compound or as separate instrumental words.

One might object that a friend should visit relatives' homes and bear their misbehavior. No, because it is hard to bear, as he says with ‘Thus.’ Even when his limbs have been cut by an enemy's arrows, he does not suffer in the same way, for he can sleep. But when pierced in his vital points by the harsh words of his own people, he burns day and night with a suffering heart.

If you think this danger cannot apply when I go there, he says: certainly, you are considered by me the favorite among the daughters of that progenitor whose standing is exalted. Even so, you will not receive honor from your father, because of your connection with me.

If one asks, ‘Lord, what have you done that Dakṣa should despise you?’ he answers: his heart, that is, his mind, is thoroughly burning and his senses are afflicted. What causes it? The prosperity, merit, fame and the like of those who witness the intellect of the person, the living self, and are free from egoism. Unable to attain their station or sovereignty, he simply hates them, as the asuras hate Hari.

One might say, ‘You indeed insulted him by failing to rise and offer respect.’ In reply: O slender-waisted one, the coming forward to greet and other formalities performed between people are rightly performed by the wise. He says in what their rightness consists: they are addressed to the Supreme Person, Śrī Vāsudeva, the indwelling Lord, and performed with the mind alone, since bodily activity is not appropriate toward the all-complete Lord. Thus I did everything mentally, seeing the indwelling Lord in him.

Moreover, homage to Vāsudeva is not made merely when visitors arrive; Vāsudeva is continually contemplated in the mind. Pure sattva means the inner faculty, or the quality sattva, and is called ‘Vasudeva.’ Why? Because in that sattva the Person Vāsudeva becomes manifest, unobscured, with his covering gone. The meaning is this: the Supreme Lord is famously called Vāsudeva because he is perceived in Vasudeva; and he is perceived in pure sattva. Thus the established meaning of the derivative determines the meaning of its base. Pure sattva is denoted by ‘Vasudeva’ through the derivations ‘that which causes the god to dwell’ or ‘that in which he dwells’ for vasu, and ‘that which shines or becomes visible’ for deva; alternatively, it shines through wealth in the form of merit. What follows? In that sattva, Lord Vāsudeva is served by my homage. In the reading ‘with the mind,’ he is especially held or contemplated by the mind. He manifests when the senses have been withdrawn below, that is, he is not an object of the senses.

‘Therefore’ means for that reason: you should not even look upon him. ‘Although he gave you your body’ distinguishes your actual father from persons called fathers figuratively because they nurture and perform other services. ‘Enemy’ means foe. He states why: O lovely-thighed one, Dakṣa disregarded me without fault when I attended the sacrifice of the creators of the world.

He declares the danger of doing otherwise. ‘Disregarding my words’ means going against them. For when a well-regarded person suffers an insult, that insult can become the cause of that person's death.
